posts.title: Why does git suck?
posts.description: English intuition vs Git's vocabulary — commit/push/add are the wrong words — plus a map into worktree essays and mailed UX critiques.
posts.html:
Git’s command names feel wrong because they are wrong for English-native intuition — and because the product never treated that mismatch as a first-class bug.

This is an overview essay. It opens on vocabulary, then branches into tighter pieces on worktrees and into a stack of critiques I have already mailed to git@vger.kernel.org. Read the worktree pair next if placement is what is burning you today.

The feely English goop

Linus and Junio are not native English speakers. That is not a gotcha biography line; it is a design constraint you can still see in the CLI.

Commands lack correct nuance. Terms overlap. The vocabulary asks you to accept a private jargon that only sometimes rhymes with ordinary English — then gaslights you when your first guess matches the dictionary and not the man page.

That goopy, ambiguous mess is not "steep learning curve" mystique. It is naming debt.

Commit, push, add — the words that should have been

git commit should be what git push is.

You commit changes from your computer to an official record. When you commit a crime, you take personal thoughts and make them part of the world. Your computer is not the world; it is local thoughts and workspace before they are publicized.

In publishing terms, that outward act is closer to publish. If the move is specifically local → public hosting service, upload is the sharper word. Today’s git commit should have been git save — the common meaning of saving a file. A local record is not official.

git add should have been git stage.

"Add" sounds like adding to existing history. To add, you have to have something; an empty stage is not something you add to. "I’m going to add a prop to the stage" is inaccurate — you put or move a prop onto the stage.

Add’s nuance: something need not have existed, or separate entities cease to be separate (cooking: add sauce to the dish, A+B becomes the dish). Indexing existing work is not changing identity through composition. Staging is.

If your fingers still type git commit and git add, fine — the muscle memory is the ecosystem. The point is the mental model Git sold you is lying about English, and that lie costs newcomers and agents alike.

gitu / git-un / git-unfuckified

I forked Git to experiment with a clearer CLI face.

Historically the fork branding is git-unfuckified, with a gitu front-end that remaps the verbs. The tree has also been referred to as git-un. Same project intent; do not treat the names as three unrelated products.

Rough gitu map (from the fork):

gitu git today Intent

save

commit

Local snapshot with a message

stage / unstage

add / reset HEAD --

Move work onto / off the stage

upload

push

Local → remote hosting

download

pull

Remote → local

history

log --oneline

Read the record

discard / undo

checkout / soft reset helpers

Back out without thesaurus gymnastics

Aliases do not absolve upstream naming. They prove the rename map is teachable.

Worktrees: the overview splits here

Vocabulary is one wound. Concurrent checkouts are another.

  • Critique: Everything wrong with Git worktrees

  • Proposal: Git worktree redesign proposal

  • Practitioner how-to (today): Org-scoped Git worktrees

  • Long-range strategy: Git worktrees long-range

Related encyclopedia framing already on the docs hub:

  • Git concurrency enshittification

  • Git’s file-shaped change model

  • VCS over FS editions

  • Concurrent agent workspaces

Critiques already mailed (git@vger)

These are my mailed critiques and notes to the Git list / personal drafts — subjects and dates, not folklore URLs. Do not treat this as a lore.kernel.org index.

Subject (approx.) Date Point in one line

git branch empty after init

2026-02-09

Fresh repos leave you staring at a branch story that feels unfinished / empty in ways newcomers should not have to research

SSH auth diagnostics when multiple ssh binaries

2025-12-09

Tooling creators own clear diagnostics; "spend a day researching which ssh" is not an acceptable UX tax

gitignore redesign (.gitignore.local, undot the name, yaml+includes, template link)

2025-11-11

Ignore rules need local overlays, honest naming, and composition — not another folklore file

gitignore include

2025-08-13

Includes so shared ignore templates compose instead of copy-paste rotting

fsmonitor—​daemon machine-wide registry for worktree sprawl orphans (draft)

2026-09-15

Worktree sprawl leaves monitor/daemon orphans; needs a machine-wide registry story

Branch switch leaving untracked artifacts → worktrees as the real fix (personal note)

2025-11-02

Switching branches scattering untracked junk is incompletely "fixed" by worktrees unless placement is conventional

What to read next

  1. Everything wrong with Git worktrees — the critique essay

  2. Git worktree redesign proposal — the constructive pair

  3. Git worktrees long-range — strategy doc

  4. Org-scoped Git worktrees — today’s agent how-to

Naming debt and placement debt are the same family of failure: Git optimized for a small circle that already knew the jargon, then scaled the jargon to the planet and to agents that invent three layouts before breakfast.

posts.title: Git worktree redesign proposal
posts.description: Default repo-local `.worktrees/<purpose>`, `git worktree add --local`, relative paths, no `.git/worktrees/` overload, porcelain discovery, migration from org-scoped hive.
posts.html:
Critique without a landing pad is just venting. Here is the constructive redesign — aligned with Git worktrees long-range and reachable from today’s org-scoped hive standard.

Pair essays: Everything wrong with Git worktrees, Why does git suck?.

Default home: <repo>/.worktrees/<purpose>

Ship a default that matches how people already want to think:

my-repo/
  .git/
  .worktrees/
    docs-pass/
    tray-fix/
  …

Short purpose slugs. Mental association with the repo. Less sibling clutter in the parent folder. Hidden .worktrees so casual directory listings stay calm.

This is the UX target. It is not free on Git as shipped today — absolute path encoding still breaks moves even when the tree is nested.

git worktree add --local

Add a first-class mode (name bikesheddable; intent is not):

git worktree add --local <purpose> [-b <branch>] <start-point>

Meaning:

  • Place under the repo’s local worktree home (default .worktrees/<purpose>).

  • Store paths relatively when the worktree lives inside the main tree.

  • Wire excludes so .worktrees/ does not pollute git status.

  • Register through the same porcelain every tool already should call.

Manual git worktree add /abs/path remains for power users. --local is how defaults stop being folklore.

Relative path storage

When a worktree is inside the main working tree (or another agreed relative root), Git should record relative links.

Absolute paths are fine for exotic placements on other volumes. They are a hazard as the only encoding for the common "purpose checkout under this repo" case. Nesting without relative storage is cosplay.

Do not overload .git/worktrees/

.git/worktrees/ stays admin metadata. User checkouts do not live there.

Optional stronger future: first-class checkout homes under .git/ only with a new reserved directory (for example .git/checkouts/<purpose>/). New name, new porcelain, same discovery channel. No puns on the metadata path.

Tool discovery via porcelain

IDEs, agents, and wrappers should discover linked trees through:

git worktree list

(and related plumbing as needed) — not through parallel layout databases, not through guessing sibling names, not through scanning for folders called worktree that might be full clones.

If discovery is porcelain-first, placement conventions become teachable without every editor inventing a second schema.

Auto exclude

Creating a local worktree home should update ignore rules (info/exclude or equivalent) so the purpose trees are not perpetual untracked noise. Humans should not hand-maintain that every time an agent adds a checkout.

Migration from today’s org-scoped hive

Today (agent compatibility):

$CODE_ROOT/<host>/<owner>/.worktrees/<repo>-<purpose-slug>

Linked only. Forbid $CODE_ROOT/.worktrees and $CODE_ROOT/worktrees. How-to: Org-scoped Git worktrees. Skill / schema live in agent-rules.

After relative/--local exists upstream (or in a fork that proves it):

  1. git worktree list from each main clone.

  2. git worktree add --local <purpose> … for active lines of work.

  3. git worktree move (or remove/re-add with care) from owner-scoped paths into repo-local homes.

  4. Prune stale admin entries; confirm monitors are not watching ghosts.

  5. Teach agents the new default; keep owner-scoped as a documented escape hatch for a while.

Migration is mechanical if discovery stayed on porcelain. It is archaeology if every agent invented a layout.

What this does not claim

This proposal does not replace filesystem editions (Phase B) — see VCS over FS editions and Git concurrency enshittification. Editions aim at stable paths with O(1) forks. Worktree redesign is the userspace bridge that stops bleeding while that matures.

It also does not rename commit/push/add. That is the vocabulary fight in Why does git suck? and the gitu / git-unfuckified / git-un experiment.

Success criteria

  • Default purpose checkouts live under <repo>/.worktrees/<purpose>.

  • --local (or equivalent) creates them with relative storage and excludes.

  • .git/worktrees/ remains metadata-only.

  • Tools discover via git worktree list.

  • Hive agents can migrate from owner-scoped without deleting unique work.

Until upstream moves, stay on the org-scoped bridge and keep pressure on the design — not on inventing a fourth folder name overnight.

posts.title: Everything wrong with Git worktrees
posts.description: Absolute paths, move breakage, agent layout chaos, sibling clutter, .git/worktrees name collision, IDE indexing, fake clones, fsmonitor orphans, and branch-switch residue.
posts.html:
git worktree is the feature teams reach for when one working tree is a lie — and then discover the feature ships without a placement contract.

This is the critique essay. Constructive redesign: Git worktree redesign proposal. Vocabulary overview: Why does git suck?.

Absolute paths are load-bearing — until you move

Linked worktrees record absolute paths in the admin metadata under .git/worktrees/ and in the per-checkout .git gitfile.

Rename a parent directory. Relocate the hive. Sync the machine to a different drive letter. The object store is fine; the links are not. Nesting the checkout under the main tree does not fix that by itself — absolute encoding is still absolute encoding.

You only get out of this class of breakage when Git can store relative paths for in-tree (or otherwise relative) worktrees. Until then, "I put it next to the repo" and "I put it inside `.worktrees`" share a fate the day the folder moves.

Agents invent inconsistent layouts

Give three agents the same prompt — "use a worktree" — and you will get siblings named repo-feature, a random directory under /tmp, a full clone mislabeled as a worktree, a hive-root $CODE_ROOT/worktrees, and a purpose folder inside the main tree that never got excluded.

Without a taught path schema, agents optimize for "the command succeeded," not for "a human can find this next week." That is how you get orphan checkouts, duplicate node_modules, and IDEs indexing four nearly identical trees.

Dev-Centr’s today answer is owner-scoped linked trees — Org-scoped Git worktrees — not because it is the aesthetic ideal, but because it is one rule agents can be graded against.

Sibling clutter vs owner-scoped vs repo-local

Sibling clutter (…/repo, …/repo-docs, …/repo-fix) is what file managers make obvious and what directories make ugly. Weak mental association. Easy for humans to create; easy for agents to create differently.

Owner-scoped ($CODE_ROOT/<host>/<owner>/.worktrees/<repo>-<purpose>) gathers every checkout for an org or user into one bucket. Longer leaf names. Not visually "inside" the repo. Compatibility bridge for hive agents. Forbids global $CODE_ROOT/.worktrees theater.

Repo-local (<repo>/.worktrees/<purpose>) is what people actually want to think: short purpose names, tight association, less peer forest. It is the long-range ideal — Git worktrees long-range — and it still needs Git features before it is safe as a default.

.git/worktrees is already taken

That path is admin metadata: per-worktree gitdirs, HEAD, commondir pointers. It is not a suggestion that your checkout should live there.

Overloading .git/worktrees/ as a user checkout home collides bookkeeping with content. Tools cannot tell "data about a worktree" from "the worktree." If Git ever wants first-class checkout homes under .git/, it needs a new reserved name (for example .git/checkouts/), not a pun on the metadata directory.

IDE and agent indexing

Every linked tree is another root for language servers, search indexes, and "open folder" habits. Path-keyed caches fork. Socket paths diverge. You paid for concurrent branches and received concurrent index thrash unless you invest in shared stores and discipline.

Agents that index the hive will happily embed three copies of the same README into context if your layout multiplies trees without a discovery convention (git worktree list, not folklore).

Dirty standalone clones mistaken for linked trees

git clone into a folder named worktrees produces an independent .git directory. It looks like concurrency. It is a second repository — second object store, second remotes story, second chance to diverge history silently.

Linked worktrees share the object store on purpose. Pretend-clones burn disk and burn trust. Any standard that does not forbid full-clone into .worktrees will be violated by the first hurried agent.

fsmonitor orphans across sprawl

Many worktrees means many paths for filesystem monitors to watch. Daemons and registries that assume one primary working tree leave orphans when trees are removed incompletely or when paths go stale after moves.

I drafted a machine-wide registry angle for fsmonitor—​daemon (2026-09-15 draft, mailed critique stack summarized in Why does git suck?). Sprawl without registry hygiene is how "worktrees fixed my branch switch" becomes "my machine watches ghosts."

Branch-switch artifacts, incompletely solved

Switching branches in one tree leaves untracked and ignored residue that does not belong to the branch you landed on. Worktrees are the honest fix for "I need two states at once."

They are an incomplete fix without placement convention: you trade branch-switch residue for path drift, sibling clutter, and monitor orphans. Personal note (2025-11-02): worktrees are the real direction — not if every tool invents a new home for them.

Where this sits in the encyclopedia

  • Git concurrency enshittification — why many live states hurt

  • Concurrent agent workspaces — worktrees / jj / GitButler tradeoffs

  • Org-scoped Git worktrees — today’s rule

  • Git worktrees long-range — target design

Next

Read the pair: Git worktree redesign proposal. Come back to the vocabulary wound anytime via Why does git suck?.

posts.title: Installation nightmares, and how to avoid them
posts.description: Installation norms as craft — FHS cargo-cult, Windows honest writes, and a dual-mode layout that might survive connectome-fs.
posts.html:
A good install is a craft problem, not a packaging trivia contest — and most install nightmares start when that craft is skipped.

This essay argues why FHS cargo-cult breaks, why Windows direct-to-disk honesty is a requirement set, and how a dual-mode layout might survive connectome-fs — philosophy first, tooling second.

Layout theater vs an install contract

A bad install, in the sense that keeps hurting users, is not always a buggy script. Often it is an unstated contract: files copied because "that is where things go," global environment mutated without a ledger, uninstall that deletes a folder but not the PATH entry that outlived it, upgrade that assumes only one version may exist because the author never side-by-side’d anything.

A good install names its claims before it writes. Machine scope vs user scope is a design choice, not a default. Side-by-side versions are a feature when your CLI promises semver. Rollback is not magic—it is knowing which registry keys, which services, which well-known names you touched.

That sounds obvious written down. It is rarely how installer templates behave, because templates optimize for the demo machine where /usr/local was empty and PATH was short.

The norms guide we are assembling tries to say the quiet part out loud: separate "where files land" from "what the install promises to the rest of the system." Land files in a tree that matches your support story. Promise the environment in a record something else can read—future you, a coordinator, a shell pin resolver.

FHS, SUS, and the cargo-cult trap

The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is useful the way a city map is useful: it orients newcomers. It is not a runtime API. Nothing in the kernel rejects your binary because you chose opt/myvendor instead of a wiki’s favorite spelling.

POSIX and the Single UNIX Specification are deeper—they stabilize behavior engineers can rely on across systems. They still do not answer the question that burns CLI authors: where does this tool live for one user on one laptop when the distro package manager, the language ecosystem, and the vendor tarball all disagree?

Cargo-cult FHS is the habit of quoting hierarchy documents without naming claims. You see it in post-install scripts that chmod +x into system directories "because Linux," in Docker images that mimic a full FHS tree for a single static binary, in debates that treat /usr/local as sin or sacrament without asking who shares that prefix on the host.

Craft means treating variance as input. Fedora’s packaging norms, Ubuntu’s Snaps, a corporate golden image, and your own ~/.local habit are different hosts. A layout that works is one whose assumptions are explicit—and whose undo path does not require guessing which of three PATH edits was yours.

Windows: direct-to-disk is not cheating

Linux people sometimes treat Windows "portable folder plus PATH" installs as immature. That judgment skips the platform’s requirement set.

MSI is a transactional, serialized mutation engine with a global lock and shared component bookkeeping. It exists because IT needed pessimistic safety more than parallel indie installs. The _MSIExecute mutex is not stupidity; it is a coarse gate chosen before your package’s file list is known. We wrote about that feeling—double-click, silence, Another installation is already in progress—in When unrelated installers still queue.

So Windows tools often write where you point them or append PATH in place with a ledger because the alternative is pretending every dev iteration is an enterprise MSI. That is not avoiding adulthood. It is matching the job: iterative CLI work wants reversibility and visibility, not a ref-count graph for a redistributable you never shared.

Craft on Windows still means the same contract: declare claims, keep undo honest, export MSI/MSIX when the deployment story requires tables and GPO—not because MSI is the only moral installer.

Linux variance without pretending one /usr

On Linux the pain is pluralism, not absence of standards. XDG gives config and data homes; binaries still scatter. Distro packages, language-specific shims, and vendor tarballs coexist on one $PATH, and tab completion breaks in proportion to how many silent mutators ran before login.

Good craft here looks like well-known entrypoint names, versioned install roots, and environment mutation you can enumerate. Bad craft looks like "we picked /usr/local/bin because the README said so" with no story for Nix users, container bind mounts, or a user who cannot sudo.

The encyclopedia cluster under installation architecture names patterns and anti-patterns so authors stop re-deriving this thread from first principles on every new tool.

UIL: one layout, two futures

The Unity Install Layout (UIL) proposal is the structural bet I want to be wrong about in the details but right about in shape.

Classic mode is today: explicit roots, side-by-side versions, ledgers for PATH and registry, entrypoints a shell can see.

Connectome mode is tomorrow’s graph: the same install as addressable content—editions, dependencies, rollback as graph operations, not only rm -rf and hope.

connectome-fs (connectome-fs.github.io) is the sibling org exploring that substrate—content-addressed storage where dependency edges can be first-class. I am not claiming your next laptop boots into a graph filesystem. I am claiming that if your install story only maps to a directory tree, you will rewrite it when graph-native storage stops being a research slide.

UIL is dual-mode so we do not fork the mental model: the manifest you author for classic paths should have a straight mapping to connectome editions. If that mapping is painful, the manifest is lying about what an install is.

Proposal write-up: Unity Install Layout (UIL). Norms checklist: Installation norms.

Shell visibility (why OpenShellOrg is in this essay)

OpenShellOrg cares about entrypoint dispatch—pins, re-exec, refusing to let the wrong Node answer when the pin said otherwise. That work only succeeds when installs are honest on the shell boundary: binaries and shims on PATH, registrations that match what landed on disk, undo that does not leave a stale shim pointing at a deleted tree.

DevCentr’s toolchain lifecycle story and OpenShellOrg’s shell-boundary story are siblings, not duplicates. We orchestrate pins and health; they stress-test whether the shell can trust what it launches. An install layout that hides binaries deep in %ProgramFiles% without a stable entrypoint is not "more secure"—it is invisible, which makes dispatch guesses and user hacks more likely, not fewer.

If you care about structured shells, treat shell-visible installs as a first-class layout requirement, not a packaging afterthought.

Tooling as hypothesis, not billboard

Docs should lead; tools should falsify the docs.

We are exploring Install Coordinator because orchestration—claims, queues, visible waits—is the gap behind pretty wizards and ugly mutex dialogs. Ibex is the host we use to try in-place PATH with ledgers, file-manager actions, and installer.kdl backends without pretending every artifact is MSI. Neither repo is the essay’s punchline. They are where we test whether the norms survive contact with Windows Explorer and CI emit.

Ibex tool docs: Ibex. Pattern comparison: Good vs bad install patterns.

What I want you to take away

Stop asking "where does FHS say?" as the first question. Ask what this install claims, who shares those resources, how undo works, and whether a shell or a graph can find the entrypoint without spelunking.

If you maintain an installer, write those answers down before the next path flamewar. If you are designing storage or dispatch, read UIL alongside connectome-fs and OpenShellOrg’s essays—same human problem, different altitude.

The guide will change when the field teaches us something new. So will this page. That is the point of inner-thought writing: the layout is a craft, not a press release.

posts.title: Auto mode is pricing theater
posts.description: Raw frontier APIs blow past a sixty-dollar IDE plan. Harness routing plus a local classify model change the spend curve.
posts.html:
Raw frontier APIs blow past a sixty-dollar IDE plan with depressing reliability. Harness routing plus a local classify model change the spend curve without shipping Python glue as the product.

A cost-and-routing essay — not a pricing announcement.

The spend curve is a routing problem

Cursor Auto is not magic intelligence. It is subsidized routing plus caching plus a willingness to spend frontier tokens only where the classifier says they earn their keep. Point Roo or Cline at Sonnet for every autocomplete and you are not competing with Auto — you are competing with the list price of a frontier model multiplied by your own context re-sends.

The escape is not a cheaper aggregator. It is not sending frontier work to the frontier.

Architect/editor splits do that by role. Mixr does it by node and job: coordinator voice, task coding, flash explore, boundary disambiguation — each with a catalog entry that can be a GLM Flash, a MiniMax agent loop, or a Kimi long-horizon run. Anthropic stays on a suppress list until someone deliberately asks for it. Nothing in my month has justified the automatic route.

On-device classify, not Python glue

The Gemini thread kept nominating RouteLLM and BERT classifiers. The useful part is the idea: a small model decides the route before the heavy model spends. The unusable part is shipping PyTorch and a Python proxy into the agent loop.

The harness default is boring on purpose: Mixr POSTs a short classify call to a local OpenAI-compatible server. If the machine is low on RAM or the server is down, we fall back. Weights can come from anywhere — convert them to whatever your runner already speaks. Glue stays out.

Lag is an architecture smell

Shadow workspaces that clone extension hosts and language servers buy first-try correctness with a second IDE in the basement. Tree-sitter driving live DOM updates buys structural awareness with reflow tax. We are not copying that stack. Speculative edits land in copy-on-write buffers; one LSP process sees synthetic URIs; tgc keeps actor threads from stop-the-worlding each other; @nogc stays on the hot patch and framing paths.

Borrow the remote UI while the harness grows

t3code already registers machines so a laptop can see conversations on a desktop. The harness does not need to reinvent that pairing story this season. It needs to be a provider that t3code can drive — session and turn over harness serve — while Mixr and the node graph grow teeth.

That is the bargain: spend like Auto without the IDE tax, suppress the models that never justify themselves, keep the router local, and let a mature remote surface babysit the harness until the desk is ready.

posts.title: Why do installers wait in line? A design failure study
posts.description: Open-source Windows installer tooling copies files well and stalls everywhere else. The global MSI lock is coarse on purpose.
posts.html:
Open-source Windows installer tooling is mature at copying files and stale everywhere else. The global MSI lock is coarse on purpose — and that is a design gap worth studying.

This essay sits beside install-coordinator work; it is not a ship note.

The free tools are not missing features. They are missing a decade.

Open a comparison matrix for Windows packaging and you will find the same names: WiX Toolset, NSIS, Inno Setup, plus Microsoft’s MSIX line and a pile of stack-specific wrappers (electron-builder, Tauri, CPack, cargo-wix). All of them can copy files, write registry keys, create shortcuts, and emit something a user can run.

What they rarely do well is the part users feel:

  • Presentation — Wizard pages with bitmap headers and system-gray chrome. Real theming — typography, motion, dark mode, frameless brand windows — means fighting the framework or embedding a full custom UI host.

  • One schema, many surfaces — GUI pages live in one place. Silent flags live in another. There is no single option model that drives wizard, CLI, and headless API equally.

  • Orchestration — Prerequisite chains, conflict detection, and queue visibility are ad hoc scripts, not first-class scheduling.

  • Observability — Structured step logs, resumable installs, explicit rollback boundaries: inconsistent at best.

Commercial tools (InstallShield, Advanced Installer) mostly win on visual authoring and enterprise deployment integration — not on a fundamentally different runtime architecture. The open-source tier is productive and visually stuck.

Inno Setup remains source-available under a custom license; since 6.5 the authors have asked commercial users to buy a license while keeping non-commercial use free. That is fair. It does not fix the UI model. WiX is the serious MSI path — XML tables, CI-friendly, enterprise-legible — and inherits every MSI constraint by design. NSIS is compact and plugin-rich and speaks a niche language your next teammate may not know.

None of them answer the question that started this thread: Why can’t two unrelated installs run at once, and what would a builder look like if it treated that as a product problem instead of an OS fact?

Three layers people conflate

The "only one installer at a time" rule is real on Windows. It is also three different mechanisms stacked on top of each other. Treating them as one blob is how you get helpless error dialogs.

Layer 1: MSI’s global _MSIExecute mutex

Microsoft’s Windows Installer holds a system-wide kernel mutex named _MSIExecute during execute sequences — and blocks concurrent API use during UI sequences too. A second MSI gets ERROR_INSTALL_ALREADY_RUNNING (1618). Microsoft documents this: \_MSIExecute Mutex.

Why it exists — and this is not mere bad engineering:

  • Transactional commit/rollback — Between InstallInitialize and InstallFinalize, MSI treats file, registry, and service changes as one atomic transaction. Two concurrent writers against overlapping system state is database concurrency without a real database underneath.

  • Shared component reference counting — MSI tracks shared DLLs and components across products. Concurrent installs can corrupt ref-count bookkeeping even when the human-visible apps look unrelated.

  • Patch ordering — MSP patches assume sequential application against a stable installed baseline.

  • Deadlock avoidance — Fine-grained locking without a global coordinator needs lock ordering, conflict detection, and rollback orchestration MSI never implemented.

The critical detail for this essay: the mutex is acquired before MSI knows whether two packages conflict. One global "installation server context" at a time — even if you are installing C:\Apps\Foo and D:\Tools\Bar with zero shared components.

Your instinct — if they only touch their own disk and registry entries, they should be able to run in parallel — is correct for provably independent MSI packages. MSI chose pessimistic simplicity in enterprise conditions where shared runtimes and SCCM-driven updates were the norm. The Visual Studio setup team ran into the same wall for automated testing and wrote about waiting on the mutex rather than failing. The lock is the explicit gate; the pain is real.

Layer 2: EXE installers that could parallelize — and often do not

NSIS and Inno do not use _MSIExecute. Multiple unrelated EXE installers can run simultaneously on Windows.

In practice you still hit walls:

  • Self-imposed mutexes — Inno’s SetupMutex, NSIS CreateMutex recipes. Authors deliberately prevent double-clicking the same installer twice, often after crash horror stories.

  • Prerequisite chains through MSI — Your "pure EXE" installer silently launches vc_redist.x64.exe. That payload is MSI. You are back in Layer 1.

  • Shared path collisions — %ProgramFiles%, %TEMP%, service names, %PATH% surgery.

  • Bootstrapper serialization — WiX Burn, custom launchers, winget, Chocolatey: orchestrators queue at their layer even when underlying payloads could overlap.

Layer 3: Enterprise and package-manager policy

Intune, SCCM, GPO software installation, and many package managers serialize by policy — one deployment at a time per machine or session — independent of MSI mechanics. That is sometimes correct (change control). Sometimes it is habit.

What a smarter runtime would declare

Imagine each install manifest declares claims instead of grabbing a global lock:

claims:
  files:
    - path: "C:/Program Files/MyApp/**"
      mode: exclusive
  registry:
    - key: "HKLM\\Software\\MyVendor\\MyApp"
      mode: exclusive
  mutex:
    - name: "Global\\MyVendor.VCRedist"
      mode: exclusive   # only this blocks peers

A coordinator acquires fine-grained locks on declared resources, queues only conflicts with visible status ("Waiting for Visual C++ Runtime…"), allows parallel non-overlapping work, and rolls back per package.

MSI cannot retrofit this easily. Its component model, transforms, patches, and _MSIExecute are baked into twenty-five years of IT tooling.

A non-MSI-first runtime could. The tradeoff: you lose native GPO/Intune MSI deployment, familiar Add/Remove Programs semantics, and admin comfort. A hybrid authoring layer — unified option schema driving GUI, CLI, and optional WiX/MSIX export — is the pragmatic shape if anyone builds this seriously.

Is there a case for a new installer builder?

Yes, if it targets orchestration and surfaces, not "yet another script-to-EXE compiler."

Strong arguments:

  1. UX gap — A modern UI host (WebView2 or equivalent) with real theming and accessibility would differentiate immediately from MUI2-era wizards.

  2. GUI ≡ CLI ≡ API — Define install options once; render pages, flags, and JSON automation from the same schema.

  3. Smart concurrency as a feature — Serialize only conflicts; show both timelines when Foo waits on VC++ and Bar proceeds. That is better than a context-free 1618 dialog.

  4. Structured install plans — Steps as a DAG with checkpoint/resume beats monolithic imperative scripts for anything beyond trivial copies.

Hard arguments — be honest:

  1. Enterprise wants MSI/MSIX — Without export paths, you are an indie developer tool, not a platform.

  2. Trust and signing — New runtimes face SmartScreen reputation cliffs.

  3. The hard parts are not UI — Elevation, reboot handling, uninstall cleanup, upgrade migrations, x64/ARM64, per-user vs per-machine, broken partial states: that is where decades of Inno/NSIS/WiX bug-fixes live.

  4. MSIX is Microsoft’s bet — Containerization sidesteps some MSI mess and introduces identity rigidity (the Third Rule of MSIX).

  5. Adoption moat — Stack defaults already point at NSIS/WiX.

We are not announcing a replacement for WiX. We are naming the gap: install orchestration with a modern UI host, resource-aware scheduling, and one option model for every surface — with optional MSI/MSIX backends when IT requires them.

Where this investigation goes next

This article freezes a working theory. The next passes will be narrower: which operations must serialize versus which are artificially blocked today; whether Easy Installer’s plugin model should grow a scheduler; what a minimal resource-claim DSL looks like in installer.kdl.

If you have war stories — double-click deadlocks, bootstrapper chains that stall on 1618, Inno mutexes you did not know you shipped — they belong in the investigation. We may revise this page or split a follow-up once the design stops being a question and starts being a spec.

  • Related shipping context: DevCentr’s new install tool, Ibex, released · MSI tables land in the generator

  • Microsoft reference: \_MSIExecute Mutex

DevCentr’s lightweight agent harness strategy is direction and design, not a News-desk release.

The sketch is a T3code-weight local agent runtime on dlang-supplemental infrastructure: harness-neutral rules, ecosystem specialization, token provenance as a first UX contract.

Why now

Open-source harnesses are useful reference implementations, but each carries its own design direction and duplicate features DevCentr already covers elsewhere in the ecosystem.

The plan is to steer upstream where it helps and integrate locally with overlap stripped — HCI Nerdz for attention and representation, Desktop-Tooling for OS utilities, dlang-supplemental for D libraries and native tooling.

First UX contract

Token provenance (HCI Nerdz) is the first harness metadata contract: mark heuristic versus grounded tokens inline so users spot assumptions like a wrong fork slug before turn three.

posts.title: Architecting your agent rules
posts.description: How to structure agent rules so harness quirks stay on the machine — and the templates stay forkable.
posts.html:
Most teams already have agent rules. The hard part is structuring them so they still make sense on the next machine, the next harness, and the next teammate’s checkout.

This piece is an architecture pass: what belongs in forkable templates, what belongs in harness config, and what belongs in workstation memory — so Cursor quirks stop leaking into the shared rules.

The moment the template stops being forkable

Picture the failure in a standup, not a diagram.

Someone opens agent-rules/AGENTS.md to add a changelog rule. The agent "helpfully" writes Z:\code\github.com\TheirName\.issues into the org skill because that is what it saw on the last machine. The PR looks fine in review—until another teammate on Linux pulls it and their agent now hallucinates paths that never existed on their box.

Or worse: the rules assume ~/.cursor/skills as if skill discovery were a law of physics. It is not. It is one harness’s convention. Another reads playbooks straight from disk. A third injects everything through a project-local file you have never heard of yet.

The template was supposed to travel. Instead it became a diary entry with YAML frontmatter.

What we split apart

Dev-Centr’s agent-rules repo always had layers on paper—portable, org, project, machine. What we had not done cleanly was treat harness behavior as its own machine-local fact, separate from workstation facts and separate from forkable policy.

So we drew a harder line:

Layer Lives in

Forkable templates

RULES.md, AGENTS.md, general/, agents/, skill bodies — placeholders only

Harness config (this machine)

$CODE_ROOT/HARNESS.md — name, skill discovery root, always-on injection slot, chat/citation behaviors

Workstation facts (this machine)

$CODE_ROOT/MEMORIES.md — tool paths, PATH gaps, hardware quirks

Project facts

<repo>/AGENTS.md + docs

Polyglot harness use is normal on one desk. You might pair Cursor with Claude Code on the same CODE_ROOT. HARNESS.md records what applies now; MEMORIES.md stays shared because ffmpeg does not care which chat window asked for it.

What the agent must do instead of guessing

We added skill harness-setup and portable modules general/harness.md + general/harness-boundary.md.

The contract is blunt:

  1. Probe the active harness—discovery hooks, always-on slot, link behavior, MCP availability.

  2. Write concrete values to $CODE_ROOT/HARNESS.md, never into upstream templates.

  3. Read general/harness-boundary.md before editing anything forkable.

If an agent is about to commit your username into a skill body, it should stop and ask which layer owns that fact. That sounds obvious. It only becomes automatic when the boundary is always-on policy, not a README footnote.

Satellite orgs: pull, don’t patch

House org init gives each banner a thin {org}/agent-rules wrapper—pointer README plus org overlay, no submodule of the canonical tree.

That means propagation is boring in the good way:

  1. Merge or pull in $CODE_ROOT/github.com/dev-centr/agent-rules

  2. Re-compose always-on rules if you use rules-manager

  3. Run harness-setup only if your harness paths changed

Wrapper repos do not need a PR for shared portable improvements unless org policy itself changed. One canonical clone, one git pull, twelve orgs breathe the same air.

Where to read the illustrated version

README slop is fine for a landing page. It is a terrible place to teach layering.

The full guide—with mermaid diagrams, setup checklist, and Cursor-as-one-example-not-the-template—is on the docs hub:

https://docs.devcentr.org/agent-rules/harness-neutral.html

Start there if you are copying these templates into another harness and want the agent to discover its own variables instead of inheriting ours.

The thesis

Other harnesses should aspire to Cursor-class features—skill discovery, local overlays, rich file links. They should not inherit Cursor’s paths baked into team policy.

Templates stay forkable when machine facts stay on the machine—and when every agent knows which file is allowed to hold them.

posts.title: After Skia: modern 2D rendering engine with Vello
posts.description: After Skia, Vello-style GPU compute is the bet for documents that grow past what Electron can carry.
posts.html:
Electron wins the ecosystem until the document grows. Then the renderer — not the feature list — decides whether an app survives two gigabytes of chat.

This is a craft note on what comes after Skia on Windows and Linux, not a product launch.

The stack you picked before you knew you needed headroom

Most desktop tools today ship as Chromium in a trench coat: Electron, or something close enough that the failure modes rhyme. You get the web stack’s superpower—every npm package, every CSS trick, every hire who has touched React—and you pay for it in processes, heaps, and layout work you never asked for.

Compare that to a retained-mode native shell (Avalonia on .NET, Qt Quick, Flutter desktop, GPUI in Rust). These draw through Skia or a successor pipeline directly to the GPU. There is no DOM tree to reflow when message number 4,000 streams in token by token. Memory still matters; GC still exists in managed runtimes—but you are not duplicating the entire web engine to render a sidebar.

The trade is real: ecosystem reach vs. baseline cost. Electron idle memory often sits in the 200–400 MB band before your app does anything interesting. A modest Avalonia or Qt shell might idle at 40–80 MB. Cold start tells the same story: browser boot vs. a single process that paints its first frame without parsing an HTML document.

None of that means "never Electron." It means know which problem you are buying.

When the document becomes the product

The pain shows up in gigabyte-scale client documents: chat, mail, live logs, repo maps with syntax highlighting on every line.

Chromium/Electron degrades because:

  1. Thousands of live DOM nodes force style recalc and reflow on every streaming update.

  2. JSON payloads cross IPC between Node and the renderer; the V8 heap balloons.

  3. Major GC pauses freeze input; OOM ends the session.

Surviving that shape requires two patterns no renderer gives you for free:

  1. Viewport windowing — only mount what is visible plus a small overdraw buffer.

  2. Off-heap history — append-only logs, SQLite, memory-mapped files; not the entire transcript as live objects in the UI heap.

Native stacks make those patterns easier. They do not remove the obligation.

The generation after "tessellate on the CPU, draw on the GPU"

Skia is not vanishing tomorrow. It still underpins Chrome, Android, Flutter’s legacy paths, Avalonia, and half the cross-platform map you already know.

But Skia’s classic Ganesh path carries twenty years of assumptions: CPU-side curve flattening, intermediate render targets, runtime shader compilation stutters. Google’s Graphite rewrite targets modern APIs—Vulkan, D3D12, Metal—with batched command buffers and pre-baked pipeline state.

Impeller is Flutter’s answer: precompiled shaders, display-list recording, less jank on mobile—and desktop paths exist, but Impeller is Flutter’s engine, not a general-purpose Skia successor you drop into arbitrary apps.

The sharper break is compute-first 2D:

  • Vello (Linebender, wgpu) pushes path filling and binning into GPU compute shaders—parallel scans instead of serial CPU tessellation. Windows via D3D12/Vulkan; Linux via Vulkan; dual-licensed Apache/MIT.

  • Rive Renderer optimizes animated vector UI with pixel-local storage tricks—MIT, embeddable.

  • Blend2D stays on CPU with JIT SIMD when GPU is absent or virtualized—Zlib.

Think in generations:

Gen 1 — CPU raster:        Cairo, GDI+, software Skia
Gen 2 — GPU tessellation:  Skia Ganesh/Graphite, Direct2D, Impeller
Gen 3 — GPU compute-first: Vello, Rive

Windows and Linux are not waiting on a mobile-only fork. Vello + wgpu is the cross-platform bet that does not require you to ship Flutter to get off CPU tessellation bottlenecks.

What I am watching (and what I am not claiming)

I am not writing a framework scorecard. Pick Avalonia if you live in .NET and want templating depth. Pick Qt if you need an industrial scene graph and C++ models. Pick GPUI if text latency and zero GC are the whole job. Pick Electron if time-to-market and web hiring dominate and your UI stays bounded.

I am claiming that renderer generation is becoming a first-class product decision—especially for tools that hold unbounded user-generated documents. Skia Graphite incrementalizes the incumbent. Vello-style compute paths rewrite the curve. Impeller proves precompiled pipelines matter—but mostly inside Flutter’s world.

All of the above are open source under permissive licenses (BSD, MIT, Apache, Zlib). The constraint is integration, not secrecy.

Where we wrote it down

The outward comparison tables, successor matrix, and desktop guidance live in the docs hub:

Graphics rendering engines — explanation

DevCentr’s toolchain advisor links there when you are targeting a desktop app or browser shell—so the mental model shows up while you are still choosing a stack, not after the heap catches fire.

posts.title: Stop translating shells
posts.description: A playbook should name the outcome. PlayTime binds how on this machine. Equivalence Engine is a catalog — not a bash-to-PowerShell blender.
posts.html:
One playbook should name what you want. PlayTime binds how on this computer. Equivalence Engine is a catalog — not a blender that turns bash into PowerShell.

Shell translation as a product goal trains people to chase syntax. Intent naming trains them to chase outcomes.

Call the file format CentrMark (.cmk). It is only writing. A playbook directive means nothing until a profile gives it a job.

Call the engine PlayTime. That name fell out of the phrase "at play time" and then earned a layer. PlayTime reads the book, learns the host, asks Equivalence Engine for a command, runs it, and writes a sidecar next to the file. It never rewrites the recipe.

Call the app Scriptbook. Today that is a CLI. Later it is also a DevCentr screen. It opens the book and talks to you. It must not become a second resolver.

The book is not the kitchen. The kitchen is not the waiter. Mixing those three is how Equivalence Engine grows a document runner, and how Scriptbook grows a package catalog. We already have both of those, elsewhere.

The blender we refused

Equivalence Engine already has two machines. People mash them together because they share a logo.

code is a path: library 5.15 → 6.0, apply rewrites. That is the "equivalence" story people remember.

cli and filesystem are already lookups. cli.install gh plus a host key returns a row in a catalog. There is no migration path from winget to apt. There is a table.

If we stuffed format and shell into that path — windows/winget/pwsh/msi — we would tensor two independent facts into nodes. The lattice would eat the engine. That is the hairy version. We did not take it.

Figure 1. Do not put a bash script through a blender

winget install GitHub.cli is not a bash program. It is not a pwsh program. It is argv: a program name and some arguments. Spawn it with no shell, the way a GUI button would. Then you do not need three "equivalent" rows for three coats.

Figure 2. One suitcase, no costumes

Shell still exists. Scriptbook’s shell= is for glue cells — echo, a Nushell helper, the verify step that is already portable. Catalog rows stay runtime argv unless the method really is curl | bash. That is a constraint ("this host must have bash"), not a dimension we multiply by format.

The student asked: MSI or bash?

Figure 3. Two doors is not a questionnaire

The teacher did not open either door. That is not a choice.

Same spine, different satellites

Install a CLI. Put config in the user config dir. Open port 443. Enable a background service. The graph is the same. The command bound to each node is not.

Sometimes the method grows extra steps that hang off the acquire node. AppImage wants a desktop file. MSI wants elevation. Flatpak does not want PATH surgery. That is a choice node that expands a small subgraph — not a second playbook.

Ask only the overlap: this tool’s methods on this host. If the overlap is one method, do not ask.

Figure 4. Ask only the overlap

GPU drivers and "tray app vs Windows service" are the exceptions. Do not force one graph there. Do not make the exception the engine.

The cycle that looked real

We wanted to register abstract instructions in Equivalence Engine so PlayTime could dereference them later. That is right. cli.install already is one. os.version would be another.

Then: if "find the OS version" is an intent, how does the engine pick the method for "find the OS version" without knowing the OS?

It doesn’t. That loop is real, and we do not walk it.

PlayTime is a compiled program. It already knows NT vs not. It probes PATH without shelling out to where versus which (those commands assume an OS). It freezes a Host Identity Record. Nested expansions reuse that snapshot. They do not re-detect and disagree.

os.version as a later playbook step is an ordinary dereference: print the version string, filtered by the snapshot you already have. PowerShell-on-Linux does not save the first step. $IsLinux only works if you are already inside pwsh. PlayTime is not.

Figure 5. Snapshot, then dereference

Call the bootstrap contract Host Awareness. There is no vendor get_os(). There are cousins: uname, /etc/os-release, RtlGetVersion, sw_vers. We sit on those. A hobby kernel can fill the record. Microsoft will not file a PR; we still bake a Windows probe.

WSL is not a new planet. It is Linux with a sticker.

The loop we actually wanted

CI already compiles tools.sdl to tools.json. Aim that trick at stage zero.

Humans register probe rows and intents in shared rules. CI runs Equivalence Engine as a compiler — it does not detect the GitHub runner — and writes an ordered cascade into PlayTime. The shipped binary wakes up offline. After the record exists, runtime PlayTime may call the engine for cli.install. New row → next bake → next release.

That is a ratchet, not a deadlock. Catalogs get richer. PlayTime wakes up on more machines. People write more playbooks. They register more intents. The next bake is richer.

Figure 6. Ratchet at build time

You live in the attic. You write install gh. The basement is argv. When winget flags change, you rewrite the basement. The book does not move. Because that is cheap, you write more abstract scripts instead of more shell. Vocabulary grows up. Realizations stay down.

Figure 7. Attic intents, basement argv

PlayTime sounds like an OpenShellOrg concern: argv honesty, host identity, not lying about which process you spawned. It might belong there someday. It is being built in scriptbook right now. We are not relocating the kitchen mid-service.

Figure 8. Aligned, not moved

The details — directives, sidecar fields, probe kinds, --to must stay a host alias — live in the docs. This page is the orientation: intents, not shell translation. Same book. This computer fills in the verbs.

  • Abstract playbooks (encyclopedia)

  • scriptbook · PlayTime at the shell boundary

posts.title: API key vs API token, an explainer
posts.description: Dashboard secrets keep getting sold as tokens. The wrong word keeps failing security reviews.
posts.html:
Vendors keep labeling long-lived dashboard secrets as "tokens." The costume is convenient for marketing and hostile to security reviews.

This essay draws the architectural split DevCentr is forcing into docs and Secrets Manager — and why the wrong word keeps failing audits.

A scene from every onboarding

Picture a Monday standup where someone says the integration is "using a token." Half the room hears short-lived OAuth bearer from a login flow. The other half hears the string we copied from Settings → Developers last quarter. Nobody notices the mismatch until a rotation runbook says "revoke the key" and an agent helpfully tries to refresh it like a session.

That is not pedantry. Wrong nouns pick the wrong playbook: dashboard rotate versus protocol refresh; project metering versus user consent; forever-secret versus fifteen-minute claim set.

What the words actually mean

An API key identifies the application or project making the request. It is how a platform bills you, rates you, and attributes traffic to "the Stripe integration" or "the mobile backend." It does not prove which human is pressing the buttons inside that app.

An access token—OAuth access token, JWT bearer, session token—identifies an authorized subject for a limited time. It answers what this holder may do now, often with scopes and an expiry baked into the credential (or into the introspection service behind it).

Hold the analogies for a second and you can feel the difference in your hands:

  • The API key is the project’s driver’s license. The meter knows which fleet car pulled up.

  • The access token is a hotel keycard. It opens these floors for this stay. Morning checkout is a feature, not a bug.

How "token" ate the dashboard

OAuth taught a generation of engineers that scoped access arrives as an access token. Cloud consoles borrowed the word for a different product: long-lived secrets you mint yourself, optionally with checkbox scopes, optionally revoked one-by-one without nuking the whole account.

So the industry grew a middle creature—scoped API keys, often sold as personal access tokens (PATs)—and dressed it in token language because:

  • scopes made it feel like OAuth,

  • Bearer headers made it travel like OAuth,

  • and "token" sounded newer and safer than the grim old "API key" that once meant a single immortal string for the entire account.

Useful product evolution. Terrible vocabulary.

Under the hood you still have two architectures:

  • Scoped key / PAT — long-lived, dashboard-born, manually revoked, project- or account-bound with capability limits.

  • True access token — handshake-born, short TTL, subject-bound, refreshed by protocol rather than by a human with a clipboard.

The rule we are enforcing

Ignore the button. Ask three questions:

  1. Was this pasted from a settings page, or minted by a login / client-credentials handshake?

  2. Does it expire in minutes or hours by design, or only when someone deletes it?

  3. Does it authorize a user or session, or only identify a project for metering?

Dashboard paste + manual revoke → API key (scoped or not). Handshake + TTL → access token (and keep refresh token for the minting secret, not for ordinary API calls).

In Secrets Manager kinds we write that as api_key, scoped_api_key, access_token, and refresh_token. Vendor aliases can live in notes for search. They do not get to own the type field.

Why Dev-Centr is picking this fight

We distribute secrets for a living—vendor → vault → local env → hosting matrix—and agents already hallucinate env names when the nouns wobble. If the UI says "token" and the architecture says "key," the agent will under-rotate forever-strings or over-store live session material. Security reviews then argue about words instead of blast radius.

So the docs tell the truth, the product forces the kinds, and this post is the public notice: stop calling keys tokens just because a dashboard did.

The costume can stay on the marketing site. It does not get into our registry.

posts.title: Search and back up from the source
posts.description: Why catalogs and backups should come from the place that hosts the software — not from a scrape of its website.
posts.html:
If you want to find a project or keep a copy of it, the honest place to ask is the host that already has it — the forge, the registry, the provider — not a third-party scrape of HTML.

This is still a vision with a near-term archive wedge, not a launched service. Treat it as orientation for the problem while the implementation catches up.
